{{Short description|Array containing every possible matrix of size m × n}}
[[File:de_bruijn_torus_3x3.stl|thumb|250px|[[STL (file format)|STL]] model of de Bruijn torus {{math|(16,32;3,3){{sub|2}}}} with 1s as panels and 0s as holes in the mesh &ndash; with consistent orientation, every {{math|3×3}} matrix appears exactly once {{viewstl|De_bruijn_torus_3x3.stl|bgcolor=black}}]]

In [[combinatorics|combinatorial]] mathematics, a '''De Bruijn torus''', named after Dutch mathematician [[Nicolaas Govert de Bruijn]], is an [[matrix (mathematics)|array]] of symbols from an alphabet (often just 0 and 1) that contains every possible [[matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] of given dimensions {{math|''m'' × ''n''}} exactly once.  It is a [[torus]] because the edges are considered wraparound for the purpose of finding matrices. Its name comes from the [[De Bruijn sequence]], which can be considered a special case where {{math|1=''n'' = 1}} (one dimension).

One of the main open questions regarding De Bruijn tori is whether a De Bruijn torus for a particular alphabet size can be constructed for a given {{mvar|m}} and {{mvar|n}}.  It is known that these always exist when {{math|1=''n'' = 1}}, since then we simply get the De Bruijn sequences, which always exist. It is also known that "square" tori exist whenever {{math|1=''m'' = ''n''}} and even (for the odd case the resulting tori cannot be square).<ref>

The smallest possible binary "square" de Bruijn torus, depicted above right, denoted as {{math|(4,4;2,2){{sub|2}}}} de Bruijn torus (or simply as {{math|''B''{{sub|2}}}}), contains all {{math|2×2}} binary matrices.

==''B''<sub>2</sub>==
[[File:2-2-4-4-de-Bruijn-torus.svg|thumb|upright|class=skin-invert-image|The (4,4;2,2) de Bruijn torus. Each 2-by-2 binary matrix can be found within it exactly once.]]
Apart from "translation", "inversion" (exchanging 0s and 1s) and "rotation" (by 90 degrees), no other {{math|1=(4,4;2,2)<sub>2</sub>}} de Bruijn tori are possible &ndash; this can be shown by complete inspection of all 2<sup>16</sup> binary matrices (or subset fulfilling constrains such as equal numbers of 0s and 1s).<ref>
{{cite journal|title=The Binatorix B2.|last1=Eggen|first1=Bernd R.|journal=Private Communication|year=1990}}
</ref>
[[File:de_bruijn_torus_3x2.svg|thumb|upright|De Bruijn torus (8,8;3,2) containing all 64 possible 3-row × 2-column matrices exactly once, with wrap&shy;around &ndash; the bottom half is the negative of the top half]]

==Larger example: ''B''<sub>4</sub>==
[[File:Visualisation of a (256,256;4,4) 2 de Bruijn torus.svg|thumb|right|260px|B<sub>4</sub> as a binary square matrix<br>The grid highlights some of the 4×4 matrices, including those [[Zero matrix|of zeros]] and [[Matrix of ones|of ones]] at the upper margin.]]
An example of the next possible binary "square" de Bruijn torus, {{math|1=(256,256;4,4)<sub>2</sub>}} (abbreviated as ''B''<sub>4</sub>), has been explicitly constructed.<ref>
{{cite journal|title=Decoding de Bruijn arrays constructed by the FFMS method.|last1=Shiu|first1=Wai-Chee|journal=Ars Combinatoria|volume=47|issue=17|year=1997|pages=33–48}}
</ref>

The image on the right shows an example of a {{math|1=(256,256;4,4)<sub>2</sub>}} de Bruijn torus / array, where the zeros have been encoded as white and the ones as red pixels respectively.

==Binary de Bruijn tori of greater size==
The paper in which an example of the {{math|1=(256,256;4,4)<sub>2</sub>}} de Bruijn torus was constructed contained over 10 pages of binary, despite its reduced font size, requiring three lines per row of array.

The subsequent possible binary de Bruijn torus, containing all binary {{math|1=6×6}} matrices, would have {{math|1=2<sup>36</sup> = 68,719,476,736}} entries, yielding a square array of dimension {{math|1=262,144×262,144}}, denoted a {{math|1=(262144,262144;6,6)<sub>2</sub>}} de Bruijn torus or simply ''B''<sub>6</sub>. This could easily be stored on a computer&mdash;if printed with pixels of side 0.1 mm, such a matrix would require an area of approximately 26×26 [[square metre|square metres]].

The object ''B''<sub>8</sub>, containing all binary {{math|1=8×8}} matrices and denoted {{math|1=(4294967296,4294967296;8,8)<sub>2</sub>}}, has a total of 2<sup>64</sup> ≈ 18.447×10<sup>18</sup> entries: storing such a matrix would require 18.5 exabits, or 2.3 [[exabyte]]s of storage. At the above scale, it would cover 429×429 [[square kilometre|square kilometres]].

==Applications==
{{Anoto_paper_principle.svg}}
De Bruijn tori are used in the spatial coding context, e.g. for localization of a camera,<ref>Szentandrási, I., Zachariás, M., Havel, J., Herout, A., Dubská, M., Kajan, R.:
 Uniform Marker Fields: Camera Localization By Orientable De Bruijn Tori. IEEE
 International Symposium on Mixed and Augmented Reality (ISMAR), pp. 319-320
 (2012).</ref> a robot<ref>Scheinerman, E.R.: Determining Planar Location Via Complement-Free de Bruijn Sequences Using Discrete Optical Sensors. IEEE Transactions on Robotics and
 Automation, 17(6), pp. 883–889 (2001).</ref> or a tangible<ref>Schüsselbauer, D., Schmid, A:, Wimmer, R.: Dothraki: Tracking Tangibles Atop Tabletops Through De-Bruijn Tori. 15th Conference on Tangible, Embedded, and Embodies Interaction (2021).</ref> based on some optical ground pattern.

They are also used as basis of the PuzzleBoard,<ref>Stelldinger, P., Schönherr, N., Biermann, J.: PuzzleBoard: A New Camera Calibration Pattern with Position Encoding, German Conference on Pattern Recognition (2024).</ref> an optical camera calibration target which adds position encoding to a chessboard calibration pattern.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://users.informatik.haw-hamburg.de/~stelldinger/pub/PuzzleBoard/ | title=PuzzleBoard: A Checkerboard Target with Lightweight Position Encoding }}</ref>
[[File:PuzzleBoard8x11.jpg|thumb|center|300px|alt=An example of a PuzzleBoard pattern with 8x11 chessboard corners.|An example of a PuzzleBoard pattern with 8x11 chessboard corners. Each 3x3 tile pattern is unique.]]

De Bruijn tori can be used to implement [[digital paper]], similar to the [[Anoto]] system. Each Anoto cell has four possible states and is thus based on a de Bruijn torus like structure with alphabet size 4. It uses a repeating 6-bit De Bruijn sequence with different offsets as columns.<ref>http://infoscience.epfl.ch/server/api/core/bitstreams/7db48a9d-e0db-424b-94f7-c5ef897c28f3/content</ref>
